title: Redundant Connection
statement: A tree with `n` nodes (labelled `1 … n`) had **one extra edge** added to it. You are given all `n` edges. Return the edge that can be removed so that the rest is a tree again; if there are several candidates, return the one that appears **last** in the input.

example.why: 1–2, 2–3 and 3–4 already connect node 1 with node 4, so the edge 1–4 closes a cycle.

idea: Add the edges one at a time and keep track of which nodes are **already connected** to each other (which *group* each node is in).

An edge between two nodes of **different** groups is useful: it merges the groups. An edge between two nodes of the **same** group adds a second route between them — a cycle. That is the redundant edge.
Union-Find stores the groups cheaply: every node points to a parent, and following parents leads to the group's **root**. Same root ⇔ same group. `union` simply makes one root point at the other.

complexity.timeWhy: One find/union pair per edge. With path compression alone each one costs O(log n) amortised — in practice almost constant. (Adding union by rank brings the total down to O(n · α(n)).)

steps.text: Our example: **`edges = [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4],[1,4],[1,5]]`**. Each step runs one highlighted line of the code.
Every node starts alone in its own group: `parent[x] = x`. A node that is its own parent is a **root** (green) and names its group. Index 0 is unused because nodes are numbered from 1.
